To date, most of the alloys used in AM are commercial grades that have been previously optimized for different manufacturing techniques. This study aims to design new alloys specifically tailored for AM processes, to minimize defects in the final products and to optimize their properties. A computational approach is proposed to design novel and optimized austenitic alloy compositions. This method integrates a suite of predictive tools, including machine learning, calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) and physical models, all piloted by a multi-objective genetic algorithm. Within this framework, several material-dependent criteria are examined and their impact on properties and on the occurrence of defects is identified. To validate our approach, experimental tests are performed on a selected alloy composition: powder is produced by gas atomization and samples are fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has been extensively studied in recent decades. Despite the significant progress achieved in manufacturing complex shapes and structures, challenges such as severe cracking when using existing alloys for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) AM have persisted. These challenges arise because commercial alloys are primarily designed for conventional casting or forging processes, overlooking the fast cooling rates, steep temperature gradients and multiple thermal cycles of L-PBF. To address this, there is an urgent need to develop novel alloys specifically tailored for L-PBF technologies. This review provides a comprehensive summary of the strategies employed in alloy design for L-PBF. It aims to guide future research on designing novel alloys dedicated to L-PBF instead of adapting existing alloys. The review begins by discussing the features of the L-PBF processes, focusing on rapid solidification and intrinsic heat treatment. Next, the printability of the four main existing alloys (Fe-, Ni-, Al- and Ti-based alloys) is critically assessed, with a comparison of their conventional weldability. It was found that the weldability criteria are not always applicable in estimating printability. Furthermore, the review presents recent advances in alloy development and associated strategies, categorizing them into crack mitigation-oriented, microstructure manipulation-oriented and machine learning-assisted approaches. Lastly, an outlook and suggestions are given to highlight the issues that need to be addressed in future work.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM), also known as 3D printing, is a disruptive manufacturing technology in which complex engineering parts are produced in a layer-by-layer manner, using a high-energy heating source and powder, wire or sheet as feeding material. The current paper aims to review the achievements in AM of steels in its ability to obtain superior properties that cannot be achieved through conventional manufacturing routes, thanks to the unique microstructural evolution in AM. The challenges that AM encounters are also reviewed, and suggestions for overcoming these challenges are provided if applicable. We focus on laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition as these two methods are currently the most common AM methods to process steels. The main foci are on austenitic stainless steels and maraging/precipitation-hardened (PH) steels, the two so far most widely used classes of steels in AM, before summarising the state-of-the-art of AM of other classes of steels. Our comprehensive review highlights that a wide range of steels can be processed by AM. The unique microstructural features including hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates induced by AM result in enhancements of strength, wear resistance and corrosion resistance of AM steels when compared to their conventional counterparts. Achieving an acceptable ductility and fatigue performance remains a challenge in AM steels. AM also acts as an intrinsic heat treatment, triggering ‘in situ’ phase transformations including tempering and other precipitation phenomena in different grades of steels such as PH steels and tool steels. A thorough discussion of the performance of AM steels as a function of these unique microstructural features is presented in this review.

Abstract:
This paper aims to review some important microstructural defects arising in the alloys manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) or laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). During the manufacturing process, various defects can occur in metals, which can negatively impact their mechanical properties and structural integrities. These defects include gas pores, lack of fusions, keyholes, melt pools, cracks, inclusions, and segregations. In this review, heterogeneities such as inclusion and segregation defects are discussed. Other types of defects have been comprehensively discussed in other reviews. Inclusions refer to foreign ceramic particles that are present within the metal, whereas segregations refer to the uneven distribution of alloying elements within the microstructure of the metal. The cause of appearance, effect of different parameters, and methods to reduce them in the final part are also reviewed. The effects of these defects on the integrity of the produced parts are discussed. Solutions for the elimination or minimization of these defects are also suggested. Post treatments and modifications of an alloy’s composition can also help to improve its material properties and reduce its defect concentration.

The results show a very fine microstructure with visible melt pool boundaries and austenite as the predominant phase. Extremely fine sub-grain structures can be found within the grains, consisting of colonies of round or elongated cellular structures depending on orientations. Due to the prevailing cooling and solidification conditions, micro-segregations occur, leading to enrichment of the sub-grain boundaries with alloying elements such as silicon, chromium, manganese and molybdenum. The presence of ferrite could be detected in this area using TEM analysis.

Abstract:
This work aims to show the impact of the allowed chemical composition range of AISI 316L stainless steel on its processability in additive manufacturing and on the resulting part properties. ASTM A276 allows the chromium and nickel contents in 316L stainless steel to be set between 16 and 18 mass%, respectively, 10 and 14 mass%. Nevertheless, the allowed compositional range impacts the microstructure formation in additive manufacturing and thus the properties of the manufactured components. Therefore, this influence is analyzed using three different starting powders. Two starting powders are laboratory alloys, one containing the maximum allowed chromium content and the other one containing the maximum nickel content. The third material is a commercial powder with the chemical composition set in the middle ground of the allowed compositional range. The materials were processed by laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M). The powder characteristics, the microstructure and defect formation, the corrosion resistance, and the mechanical properties were investigated as a function of the chemical composition of the powders used. As a main result, solid-state cracking could be observed in samples additively manufactured from the starting powder containing the maximum nickel content. This is related to a fully austenitic solidification, which occurs because of the low chromium to nickel equivalent ratio. These cracks reduce the corrosion resistance as well as the elongation at fracture of the additively manufactured material that possesses a low chromium to nickel equivalent ratio of 1.0. A limitation of the nickel equivalent of the 316L type steel is suggested for PBF-LB/M production. Based on the knowledge obtained, a more detailed specification of the chemical composition of the type 316L stainless steel is recommended so that this steel can be PBF-LB/M processed to defect-free components with the desired mechanical and chemical properties.

Abstract:
In the rapidly evolving field of additive manufacturing (AM), the predictability of part properties is still challenging due to the inherent multiphysics complexity of the technology. This results in time-consuming and costly experimental guess-and-check approaches for manufacturing each individual design. Through synthesising advancements in the field, this review argues that numerical modelling is instrumental in mitigating these challenges by working in tandem with experimental studies. Unique hierarchical microstructures induced by extreme AM process conditions– including melt pool patterns, grains, cellular–dendritic substructures, and precipitates—affect the final part properties. Therefore, the development of microstructure-informed mechanical models becomes vital. Our review of numerical studies explores various modelling approaches that consider the microstructural features explicitly and offers insights into multiscale stress–strain analysis across diverse materials fabricated by powder bed fusion AM. The literature indicates a growing consensus on the key role of multiscale integrated process–structure–property–performance (PSPP) modelling in capturing the complexity of AM-produced materials. Current models, though increasingly sophisticated, still tend to relate only two elements of the PSPP chain while often focusing on a single scale. This emphasises the need for integrated PSPP approaches validated by a solid experimental base. The PSPP paradigm for AM, while promising as a concept, is still in its infantry, confronting multifaceted challenges that require in-depth, multidisciplinary expertise. These challenges range from accounting for multiphysics phenomena (e.g., advanced laser–material interaction) and their interplay (thermo-mechanical and microstructural evolution for simulating Type II residual stresses), accurately defined assumptions (e.g., flat molten surface during AM or purely epitaxial solidification), and correctly estimated boundary conditions for each element of the PSPP chain up to the need to balance the model’s complexity and detalisation in terms of both multiphysics and discretisation with efficient multitrack and multilayer simulations. Efforts in bridging these gaps would not only improve predictability but also expedite the development and certification of new AM materials.

Abstract:
Inconel 738LC (IN738LC) is a nickel-based superalloy specially used in the hot section components of turbine engines. One of its main drawbacks relies on the cracking susceptibility when it is manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). This paper analyzes the influence of minor alloying element concentration on cracking tendency of IN738LC superalloy manufactured by LPBF. For that objective, samples were manufactured using two powders, which presented different minor alloying elements concentration (Si, Zr and B). It was shown that the samples crack tendency was very different depending on the powder used for their manufacturing. In fact, the measured crack density value was 2.73 mm/mm2 for the samples manufactured with the powder with higher minor alloying elements concentration, while 0.25 mm/mm2 for the others. Additionally, a special emphasis has been put on elemental composition characterization in cracked grain boundaries in order to quantify possible Si or Zr enrichment. It has been also studied the differences of solidification ranges and grain structures between both samples as a consequence of different minor alloying elements concentration in order to analyze their effect on crack susceptibility. In this sense, Scheil-Gulliver simulation results have shown that samples with higher Si and Zr contents presented higher solidification range temperature. This fact, as well as an increase of the presence of high angle grain boundaries (HAGB), leaded to an increment in the crack formation during solidification. Therefore, in this research work, an understanding of the factors affecting crack phenomenon in the LPBF manufactured IN738LC was accomplished.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Throughout recent years, the implementation of nanoparticles into the microstructure of additively manufactured (AM) parts has gained great attention in the material science community. The dispersion strengthening (DS) effect achieved leads to a substantial improvement in the mechanical properties of the alloy used. In this work, an ex situ approach of powder conditioning prior to the AM process as per a newly developed fluidized bed reactor (FBR) was applied to a titanium-enriched variant of the NiCu-based Alloy 400. Powders were investigated before and after FBR exposure, and it was found that the conditioning led to a significant increase in the TiN formation along grain boundaries. Manufactured to parts via laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), the ex situ FBR approach not only revealed a superior microstructure compared to unconditioned parts but also with respect to a recently introduced in situ approach based on a gas atomization reaction synthesis (GARS). A substantially higher number of nanoparticles formed along cell walls and enabled an effective suppression of dislocation movement, resulting in excellent tensile, creep, and fatigue properties, even at elevated temperatures up to 750 °C. Such outstanding properties have never been documented for AM-processed Alloy 400, which is why the demonstrated FBR ex situ conditioning marks a promising modification route for future alloy systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing of lightweight metallic alloys, particularly aluminum- and titanium-based systems, has emerged as a transformative approach for producing high-performance components with unprecedented design freedom. Among available technologies, laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) offers superior geometrical resolution and microstructural control; however, the successful processing of lightweight alloys remains constrained by fundamental challenges related to printability, defect formation, and microstructural heterogeneity. This review critically examines the process–structure–property relationships governing L-PBF fabrication of aluminum and titanium alloys, with a specific focus on the mechanisms of defect generation and their implications for mechanical performance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>First, the unique thermophysical characteristics of lightweight alloys—including high reflectivity, oxidation tendency, and rapid solidification kinetics—are analyzed in the context of melt pool dynamics and thermal gradients. Second, alloy-specific microstructural evolution is discussed, highlighting the formation of cellular structures in Al–Si systems and martensitic transformations in Ti–6Al–4 V, alongside their dependence on process parameters. Third, the dominant defect mechanisms, including lack-of-fusion porosity, keyhole-induced voids, hydrogen gas porosity, and hot cracking, are systematically compared between aluminum and titanium alloys, establishing clear cause–effect relationships between processing conditions and structural integrity.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Building upon these insights, the review integrates recent advances in computational modeling approaches—such as CALPHAD, phase-field simulations, and machine learning—to demonstrate how predictive frameworks can guide alloy design and process optimization. A cross-material comparison is further developed to identify critical differences and shared limitations in printability and performance. Finally, a unified design strategy is proposed, linking process control, alloy chemistry, and defect mitigation to enable the development of next-generation lightweight materials tailored for additive manufacturing.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This work provides a focused and analytical perspective that bridges fundamental mechanisms with practical design strategies, offering a roadmap for advancing lightweight alloy applications in aerospace, automotive, and energy sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Complex structures can now be manufactured easily utilizing AM technologies to meet the pre-requisite objectives such as reduced part numbers, greater functionality, and lightweight, among others. Polymers, metals, and ceramics are the few materials that can be used in AM technology, but metallic materials (Magnesium and Aluminum) are attracting more attention from the research and industrial point of view. Understanding the role processing parameters of laser-based additive manufacturing is critical to maximize the usage of material in forming the product geometry. LPBF (Laser powder-based fusion) method is regarded as a potent and effective additive manufacturing technique for creating intricate 3D forms/parts with high levels of precision and reproducibility together with acceptable metallurgical characteristics. While dealing with LBPF, some degree of porosity is acceptable because it is unavoidable; hot ripping and cracking must be avoided, though. The necessary manufacturing of pre-alloyed powder and ductility remains to be the primary concern while dealing with a laser-based additive manufacturing approach. The presence of the Al-Si eutectic phase in AlSi10Mg and AlSi12 alloy attributing to excellent castability and low shrinkage, attaining the most attention in the laser-based approach. Related studies with these alloys along with precipitation hardening and heat treatment processing were discussed. The Pure Mg, Mg-Al alloy, Mg-RE alloy, and Mg-Zn alloy along with the mechanical characteristics, electrochemical durability, and biocompatibility of Mg-based material have been elaborated in the work-study. The review article also summarizes the processing parameters of the additive manufacturing powder-based approach relating to different Mg-based alloys. For future aspects, the optimization of processing parameters, composition of the alloy, and quality of powder material used will significantly improve the ductility of additively manufactured Mg alloy by the LPBF approach. Other than that, the recycling of Mg-alloy powder hasn’t been investigated yet. Meanwhile, the post-processing approach, including a homogeneous coating on the porous scaffolds, will mark the suitability in terms of future advancements in Mg and Al-based alloys.

The objective of this review is to emphasize the key challenges in developing and performing in situ X-ray imaging of solidification processes, as well as to highlight important contributions that have significantly advanced the understanding of various mechanisms pertaining to microstructural evolution, defects, and semi-solid deformation of metallic alloy systems. Finally, a discussion on the recent breakthroughs in the emerging technology of additive manufacturing, and the challenges thereof, are presented.

## 3. A Novel Methodology for the Thermographic Cooling Rate Measurement during Powder Bed Fusion of Metals Using a Laser Beam

Abstract:
Powder bed fusion of metals using a laser beam (PBF-LB/M) is a process that enables the fabrication of geometrically complex parts. In this process, a laser beam melts a metallic powder locally to build the desired geometry. The melt pool solidifies rapidly, which results in high cooling rates. These rates vary during the process in line with the geometric characteristics of the part, which leads to a non-uniform microstructure along with anisotropic mechanical properties. The unknown part characteristics prevent the process from being used in safety-critical applications. Thermographic in situ process monitoring provides information about the thermal field, enabling predictions of the resulting material properties. This study presents a novel methodology for the thermographic measurement of cooling rates during the PBF-LB/M process using a high-speed thermographic camera. The cooling rates occurring during the manufacturing of 316L tower-like specimens were measured. The cooling rate decreased with increasing build height, due to the heat accumulation in the parts. The microhardness profile of the parts was tested perpendicularly and parallel to the build direction. A significant decrease in hardness values was observed along the build height. The measured cooling rate was correlated to the microhardness profile of the specimens using a Hall–Petch type relationship. The results show a high level of reproducibility of the cooling rates between different specimens in the same build job as well as between subsequent build jobs. The presented methodology allows studying the effects of the geometry on the cooling rates and the resulting mechanical properties of 316L specimens.

## pqac-00000042

From text 'hasenbusch2023acomparisonof pages 19-29'.

Zachary Arthur Hasenbusch, Andrew Deal, Ben Brown, Davis Wilson, Laurentiu Nastac, and Luke N Brewer. A comparison of solidification structures and submicroscale cellular segregation in rapidly solidified stainless steels produced via two-piston splat quenching and laser powder bed fusion. Microscopy and Microanalysis, 29:1328-1349, Jul 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1093/micmic/ozad065, doi:10.1093/micmic/ozad065. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides related LPBF 316L observations but does not identify or report the Krakhmalev (2018) atom probe tomography (APT) dataset specifically. STEM-EDX measurements in the LPBF alloy-1 austenitic (type 1) cells found enrichment of Cr and Mo at cell boundaries, accompanied by reduced Fe signal; Ni is listed among the analyzed elements, but the excerpt does not state that Ni segregated. The reported solidification-cell diameters for both LPBF and splat-quenched material were approximately 0.20–0.40 µm, corresponding to estimated cooling rates of 9.3 × 10^6–7.7 × 10^7 K/s and solidification rates of about 390–830 mm/s. Within the melt pool, type 1 cells occurred near the bottom edge, where cooling and solidification rates were fastest, while type 2 cells occurred toward the interior/top, where rates were lower. The excerpt also states that LPBF produced a larger average cell size than splat quenching, but it does not provide a detailed numerical LPBF-only spacing profile or explicit APT Cr-Mo-Ni concentrations.

2. Experimental procedures         Pre-proof
  AM samples of a size of 30 × 30 × 30 mm3 were built in an industrial machine (EOSINT

according to ISO/ASTM 529000:2017. The AM parameters were set to those proposed by

the manufacturer and were as follows: laser power 285 W, laser speed 960 mm/s. The    Journal

distance between the laser paths was 0.11 mm, with a laser diameter of 0.055 mm. The

hatching occurred in the x and y directions, using alternating and rotating modes. The

samples were fabricated in a nitrogen atmosphere of 99.5 % purity. The microstructure and

mechanical properties were studied on as-deposited material in the building direction. The

microstructure was probed at several positions to ensure the structural homogeneity. The

mechanical properties were measured on small, standard, dog-bone tensile specimens, with

were made by, first, remelting 316L stainless steel in a laboratory induction furnace and

then casting ingots into metallic moulds. The as-cast specimens were investigated with no

further treatment. Parts of the ingots were further hot forged starting at 850 °C using a

laboratory hammer device, thereby simulating industrial conditions. The final step was a

recrystallization and  solution treatment  at 1040° C  for 30 minutes.  In  addition  to

recrystallization this treatment removed the stresses occurring during cold-working and

homogenized the dendritic structure. The chemical compositions of the different samples

are compiled in Table 1.         Pre-proof

(20 ml glycerine, 10 ml HNO3, 30 ml HCl). To reveal the melt pool lines only, the specimens

samples [26]. ECCI enables the observation of much larger areas of a specimen than a TEM

does. In this study ECCI was performed on a Zeiss Merlin SEM operated at 30 kV and with a

beam current of 2 nA. The sample was at a working distance of 7 mm and a retractable 4-

quadrant BSE detector was used.    Journal  The structure and composition of the sample was also investigated by scanning-

transmission electron microscopy (STEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) and

from the bulk polished material. Special attention was paid to target a sample position that

3.1. Microstructure vs. mechanical properties

affected by the manufacturing method. A comparison of the microstructures of AM, as-cast

and forged steel samples  is shown in  Fig. 1.  It can be seen that the AM industrial

manufacturing procedure results in characteristic reversed-bell-like grains.

Figure 1. EBSD IPF Z micrographs of three different processed stainless steel AISI 316L
samples, (a) additive manufactured, (b) forged, (c) as-cast.  The light microscopeJournalimage (Fig. 1 a inset) shows a clear indication of the melt pools

produced by the laser melting of the precursor powder. The melt-pool boundaries are

visible using the optical microscope upon etching the sample, which could imply either a

structure develops hierarchically. The nucleation starts sporadically at the bottom of the

melt pool, where the grain either follows the same orientation or develops a different one.

The elongated dendrites grow mostly in the deposition direction, which correlates with the

radial (Fig. 8 b). Due to the complex thermal environment, some of the dendrites can

In these experiments, the effect of energy density on melt pool depth was probed for two

plates were prepared with 50 µm thick powder layers. A top view of a build plate is shown in

After the tracks were produced, the loose powder was removed from the plates. Top-view

made. The plates were then sectioned. For each polished and etched cross section,


measurements were made of the width of the track, the height of the track above the build

and the area of the track into the build plate.



3.3.2.  Synchrotron Radiation Micro-Tomography


Synchrotron Radiation micro-Tomography (SRµT) was used to visualize the three-


dimensional void distribution in a sectioned track. A track with parameters 137 W power,

188 mm/s scan speed, and D4σ =52 µm was selected for imaging because it displayed

evidence of keyhole-mode laser melting during metallurgical investigation. The sample was

machined from the track to the dimensions 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm × 10 mm using a low-speed


saw. The dimensions were selected in order to incorporate as much of the keyhole region


while still maintaining good X-ray transmission through the sample. Specifically, one of the1.3 mm sides was centered at the track and the 10 mm side started at the weld surface and


extended downward in a direction corresponding to the depth of the melt pool.


  The tomographic imaging was performed at beamline 8.3.2 at the Advanced Light Source


(Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, USA) in white-light mode to obtain the


maximum flux and intensity. The experimental setup was similar to standard tomographic


procedures (Kinney and Nichols, 1992) where the sample is rotated in an X-ray beam and the


transmitted radiographic projections are imaged via a scintillator, magnifying lens, and a

digital camera. For this experiment, the effective voxel size was 1.3 µm × 1.3 µm × 1.3 µm.


Reconstructed images were obtained via a filtered back-projection algorithm using the


Octopus software (Vlassenbroeck et al., 2007). Three-dimensional visualization and

quantification of the void distribution was performed using the Avizo™ software (Mercury,

4. Simulation methods



   In the experiments, there is the potential for significant scatter due to variations in the


melt pool depth. Simulations were carried out to aid in determining whether any scatter in


the data is due to these depth variations or due to shortcomings in using normalized enthalpy


to plot the data.


  The model for selective laser melting with evaporation of Verhaeghe et al. was


implemented for comparison with the experimental results (Verhaeghe et al., 2009). This


thermal model accounts for laser heating of the powder and substrate using the method


developed by Gusarov et al. and for enthalpy effects due to phase transformations (Gusarov et


al., 2009). These simulations are performed with an Eulerian grid with a moving heat source,


removing the need for upwind differencing for the conduction terms.  The allowed phase transformations on heating are powder to liquid to vapor and on cooling


are liquid to solid. As the powder melts or as liquid vaporizes, the material compacts in the


direction of gravity but not laterally. This allows for mass and enthalpy to effectively leave the


system due to vaporization; however, the model does not include the interaction of the laser


with the metal vapor or recoil pressure effects that are necessary to sustain a keyhole in the


molten metal. Because these simulations do not contain the physics necessary for keyhole


formation, it is expected that the simulation results could agree with the experimental results


in the conduction-melting regime but not necessarily in the keyhole regime.

5.1.Characteristics of conduction mode melting



Fig. 2 shows a cross section of a single-track experiment where the depth of the melt pool


was controlled by thermal conduction. When the laser impinges on the powder layer, the


laser energy is absorbed in the skin of the upper most powder particles, which melt and begin


to consolidate because of the surface tension of the molten metal. This liquid must have


sufficient enthalpy to melt the underlying powder and enough of the underlying solid


material to form a good bond. Notice that the cross section of the melt pool is semicircular as


predicted by the conduction-mode model (Eagar and Tsai, 1983).




5.2.Characteristics of keyhole mode melting



According to the model of Eagar and Tsai, the cross section of a melt pool formed in


conduction mode is about semicircular (Eagar and Tsai, 1983). That is, the melt pool depth is


about equal to its width. The occurrence of keyhole melting in this work was determined by


identifying those melt pools where the depth was greater than the half width. Micrographscorresponding to each data point were also observed and identified as being either


characteristic of conduction mode or keyhole mode (Rai et al., 2007).


  The three images in Fig. 3 are cross-sections of three different experiments carried out

under the same conditions: 150 W laser power, 100 mm/s scan speed, D4σ =52 µm. The

contrast below the surface of the build plate is representative of what is observed in keyhole-


mode laser welding where the depth of the melt pool is greater than the melt pool half-width.


In Fig. 3, the melt pool extends more than 300 µm below the surface of the build plate. Of

expected to be left in the wake of the deeply penetrating laser beam.

three-dimensional distribution of the voids represented in purple and Fig. 4(b) shows two-


dimensional tomograms of three cross sections taken at different positions in the sample


along the laser track. Each cross-section in Fig. 4(b) has a different void distribution. Fig. 4(c)


shows a three-dimensional rendering of the surface of the sample. The incomplete collapse of


the vapor cavity leaves voids in the wake of the laser beam, which is observed in Fig. 4 (a), (b),


and (c). X-ray tomography has previously been used to characterize three-dimensional pores


in stainless steel welds (Madison and Aagesen, 2012). Similar to what was found in the study


by Madison et al., the three dimensional morphology of the voids in the sample was observed


to be anisotropic and it was also found that the main contribution to overall porosity in the


sample was due to a few voids with the largest void volume.5.3.Utility of the normalized enthalpy to combine the effects of power, speed, and beam size

Felix Großwendt, Louis Becker, Arne Röttger, Abootorab Baqerzadeh Chehreh, Anna Luise Strauch, Volker Uhlenwinkel, Jonathan Lentz, Frank Walther, Rainer Fechte-Heinen, Sebastian Weber, and Werner Theisen. Impact of the allowed compositional range of additively manufactured 316l stainless steel on processability and material properties. Materials, 14:4074, Jul 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14154074, doi:10.3390/ma14154074. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt indicates that Thermo-Calc was used to calculate an Fe–Cr–Ni pseudobinary phase-diagram section at 70 mass% Fe and that Scheil–Gulliver calculations were used to represent rapid, non-equilibrium, diffusionless solidification comparable to PBF-LB/M. The Scheil paths predict primary bcc-ferrite solidification for alloys A and B, whose Creq/Nieq ratios are 1.35 and 1.43, respectively. Alloy C, with Creq/Nieq = 1.00, is predicted to solidify primarily as fcc austenite. This differs from the experimentally observed PBF microstructures: A-PBF and C-PBF were fully austenitic, while B-PBF retained only a small ferrite fraction. The discrepancy is attributed to intrinsic reheating during layer deposition, which enables diffusion and transformation of initially solidified ferrite into austenite. The provided pages do not state numerical freezing ranges from either the Scheil or equilibrium calculations, nor do they give the full elemental compositions of alloys A, B, and C. They only identify the calculation basis (Fe–Cr–Ni, 70 mass% Fe), the 316L ASTM compositional range, and the relevant Creq/Nieq ratios.

Marios P. Sotiriou, John S. Aristeidakis, Maria-Ioanna T. Tzini, Ioanna Papadioti, Gregory N. Haidemenopoulos, and Nikolaos Aravas. Microstructural and thermomechanical simulation of the additive manufacturing process in 316l austenitic stainless steel. Proceedings of The 1st International Electronic Conference on Metallurgy and Metals, pages 20, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/iec2m-09237, doi:10.3390/iec2m-09237. This article has 12 citations.

The excerpt summarizes the Thermo-Calc-based thermodynamic and kinetic analysis of 316L solidification during additive manufacturing. It states that equilibrium and non-equilibrium solidification were treated as limiting cases, with the Scheil–Gulliver model representing the non-equilibrium condition. The calculated freezing range depends on the solidification cooling rate: Scheil–Gulliver predicts the highest freezing range, whereas equilibrium solidification predicts the lowest. The passage does not provide numerical liquidus or solidus temperatures, nor does it state a numerical primary δ-ferrite fraction. It does, however, describe δ-ferrite evolution during repeated thermal cycling: the γ/δ interface moves toward the ferrite side, the δ-ferrite volume fraction gradually decreases, and equilibrium is approached. Elemental microsegregation occurs in both austenite and ferrite during thermal cycling. Cr and Ni segregation profiles become progressively narrower with successive cycles as diffusion homogenizes the phases; Cr concentration in ferrite and Ni concentration in austenite at the interface decrease during the final cycles under local equilibrium conditions. The excerpt’s conclusion refers broadly to substitutional-element microsegregation and does not separately quantify Mo segregation, although the associated figure includes concentration profiles for C, Mn, Cr, Ni, and Mo.

### 1. CALPHAD Predictions: Liquidus, Solidus, Freezing Range, and Primary Phase

**Equilibrium solidification.** Thermo-Calc calculations for 316L stainless steel using the TCFE database predict an equilibrium liquidus temperature of approximately 1453 °C and a solidus of approximately 1424 °C, yielding a freezing range of about 29 K (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000020). Sotiriou et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/iec2m-09237) used Thermo-Calc with TCFE6 for a nominal 316L composition of Fe–18Cr–14Ni–2.6Mo–1Mn–0.03C (wt%) and adopted a solidus of 1400 °C and liquidus of 1459 °C (a 59 K interval) as model inputs for their heat-transfer simulation, with a latent heat of 330 kJ/kg distributed over that range (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). These values differ from the Wahib (2024; DOI: 10.34901/mul.pub.2024.074) Thermo-Calc output because the alloy compositions and databases used are not identical—illustrating the sensitivity of CALPHAD predictions to both input chemistry and database version.

**Scheil–Gulliver solidification.** The Scheil–Gulliver model, which assumes no solid-state diffusion and complete liquid mixing, predicts a wider freezing range than equilibrium because extended solute rejection into the liquid depresses the terminal solidus temperature (pqac-00000057). Sotiriou et al. explicitly stated that the Scheil–Gulliver model yields the highest freezing range, while equilibrium gives the lowest, with DICTRA kinetic simulations falling in between depending on the imposed thermal cycle (pqac-00000057). Assi et al. (2024; DOI: 10.3390/app14198649) defined the "critical temperature range" from Scheil as the interval between 95% and 99% solid fraction, which is the most cracking-sensitive portion of the solidification path (pqac-00000061).

**Primary phase: δ-ferrite vs. austenite.** For typical mid-specification 316L compositions (Creq/Nieq ≈ 1.3–1.5), CALPHAD and Scheil calculations predict primary δ-ferrite solidification via the ferrite–austenite (FA) mode: L → L + δ → L + δ + γ → γ + δ (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031). Grosswendt et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/ma14154074) used Thermo-Calc Scheil–Gulliver simulations with an Fe–Cr–Ni pseudobinary at 70 mass% Fe and showed that alloys with Creq/Nieq = 1.35 and 1.43 solidify as primary bcc ferrite, while an alloy with Creq/Nieq = 1.00 solidifies as primary fcc austenite (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000053).

**Creq/Nieq and composition effects.** The Schaeffler equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 1.4(%Si) + 0.5(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 0.5(%Mn) + 30(%C); the WRC-1992 equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 0.7(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 35(%C) + 20(%N) + 0.25(%Cu) (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031). Within the ASTM A276 316L specification, the permissible Creq/Nieq ratio can range from as low as 1.01 to as high as 2.21, spanning fully austenitic (A) through ferritic–austenitic (FA) solidification regimes (pqac-00000033). Below approximately 1.3, fully austenitic solidification is expected; above approximately 1.49 (Schaeffler) or 1.59 (Hammar–Svensson), primary ferrite becomes dominant (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034). This is a **strongly supported** finding from multiple independent studies. Grosswendt et al. recommend restricting the Ni equivalent and setting Cr to 17–18 mass% for PBF-LB/M to maintain Creq/Nieq > 1.3 and avoid ductility-dip cracking that accompanies fully austenitic solidification (pqac-00000033).

**Retained ferrite in as-built LPBF 316L.** Despite equilibrium and Scheil predictions of primary δ-ferrite for mid-specification compositions, as-built LPBF 316L is typically fully austenitic with no detectable δ-ferrite by XRD (pqac-00000025). This is attributed to the combination of rapid solidification (cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s) and intrinsic reheating from subsequent layer deposition, which enables diffusion-driven transformation of initially solidified ferrite into austenite (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000026). Grosswendt et al. confirmed that their PBF-LB/M samples A and C were fully austenitic, while sample B retained only a small ferrite fraction (pqac-00000030). Some studies have detected trace ferrite by TEM at cell boundaries in SLM 316L (pqac-00000038), but the consensus is that the as-built phase is overwhelmingly austenitic. This represents a **strong** finding.

---

### 2. Cellular Sub-Structure: Cell Spacing vs. Cooling Rate

The solidification microstructure of LPBF 316L consists of columnar cellular sub-structures with cell spacings of approximately 0.2–0.8 µm, corresponding to estimated cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000002).

**Empirical relation.** The widely used fitted relation for stainless steels is:

λ (µm) = 80 · Ṫ⁻⁰·³³

where Ṫ is the cooling rate in K/s, a = 80 µm·(K/s)⁰·³³, and n = 0.33 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000039). This relation was used by both Fu et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102067) and Vallejo et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11050832) for LPBF 316L, with consistent results.

Bertoli et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2018.10.051) systematically varied LPBF parameters and reported the solidification conditions summarized in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

The cooling rate is inversely proportional to the P/v ratio (linear energy density), confirming that G·R ∝ v/P (pqac-00000039). The G/R ratio remained within a narrow range of 100–200 K·s/mm² across all tested conditions, which is why only columnar cellular morphology was observed—never equiaxed dendrites (pqac-00000039).

**Spatial variation within melt pools.** Cell size varies systematically within a single melt pool. Near the melt-pool boundary, where the thermal gradient G is highest and the solidification rate R is lowest, finer cells form ("type 1" cells, 0.20–0.40 µm diameter). Toward the melt-pool center/top, where cooling rates decrease, coarser cells develop ("type 2") (pqac-00000042). Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) confirmed that G/R decreases from the melt-pool boundary toward the center, promoting a gradual transition from columnar to more equiaxed morphologies (pqac-00000052). The cells have a 3D prism-like morphology with their long axes aligned along <001> crystallographic directions, and undergo 90° side-branching near melt-pool boundary intersections (pqac-00000052).

---

**Quantitative STEM-EDS data.** Godec et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074) provided the most detailed quantitative STEM-EDS measurements for LPBF 316L (EOS M280, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, nitrogen atmosphere). At the dislocation-based cell walls (position 3): Cr = 17.4 wt%, Mo = 4.2 wt%, Mn = 1.8 wt%, Ni = 13.7 wt%, Fe = 62.9 wt%. Inside the cell (position 2): Cr = 17.0 wt%, Mo = 3.3 wt%, Mn = 1.7 wt%, Ni = 13.5 wt%, Fe = 64.5 wt%. At the melt-pool boundary (position 1): Cr = 16.6 wt%, Mo = 3.1 wt%, Ni = 13.6 wt%, Fe = 64.9 wt% (pqac-00000044). Thus, Mo is the most strongly segregated element, with approximately 27% enrichment at cell walls relative to the cell interior, while Cr shows modest enrichment (~2%) and Ni is essentially uniform. The melt-pool boundary is characterized by a Mo and Cr *deficit* relative to both the cell walls and cell interiors, explaining why even minor composition differences produce a strong etching effect that makes melt-pool boundaries visible under optical microscopy (pqac-00000044).

**Comparison with Scheil predictions.** Hasenbusch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1093/micmic/ozad065) compared measured STEM-EDX segregation ratios with both classic Scheil and Scheil-with-solute-trapping models for rapidly solidified 316L-type alloys. Both Scheil variants generally **overestimated** the degree of segregation relative to experiments (pqac-00000037). This is consistent with the finding by Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) that Thermo-Calc Scheil simulations for L-PBF 316L show strong Cr and Mo segregation at the end of liquid–solid transformation, but after only 0.1 s the segregation weakens substantially, and after 1 s it is nearly absent, due to the high equilibrium partition coefficients of these elements in austenite (pqac-00000052). These particles act as Zener-pinning sites for dislocations (pqac-00000010). Funch et al. Multiple etchants have been documented for revealing cells and melt-pool boundaries in LPBF 316L:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**SEM conditions for microsegregation contrast.** Godec et al. (2020) used electron channelling contrast imaging (ECCI) with a Zeiss Merlin SEM at 30 kV, 2 nA beam current, 7 mm working distance, and a retractable 4-quadrant BSE detector to image dislocation cells and nano-inclusions in bulk polished (unetched) samples (pqac-00000043). ΔH/h_s = AP / [h_s √(π D u σ³)]

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

- Sotiriou et al. (2021), Table 1: temperature-dependent k and c_p for 316L (DOI: 10.3390/iec2m-09237)."}

(2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074) provided the most detailed quantitative STEM-EDS measurements for LPBF 316L (EOS M280, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, nitrogen atmosphere). At the dislocation-based cell walls (position 3): Cr = 17.4 wt%, Mo = 4.2 wt%, Mn = 1.8 wt%, Ni = 13.7 wt%, Fe = 62.9 wt%. Inside the cell (position 2): Cr = 17.0 wt%, Mo = 3.3 wt%, Mn = 1.7 wt%, Ni = 13.5 wt%, Fe = 64.5 wt%. At the melt-pool boundary (position 1): Cr = 16.6 wt%, Mo = 3.1 wt%, Ni = 13.6 wt%, Fe = 64.9 wt% (pqac-00000044). Thus, Mo is the most strongly segregated element, with approximately 27% enrichment at cell walls relative to the cell interior, while Cr shows modest enrichment (~2%) and Ni is essentially uniform. The melt-pool boundary is characterized by a Mo and Cr *deficit* relative to both the cell walls and cell interiors, explaining why even minor composition differences produce a strong etching effect that makes melt-pool boundaries visible under optical microscopy (pqac-00000044).

**Comparison with Scheil predictions.** Hasenbusch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1093/micmic/ozad065) compared measured STEM-EDX segregation ratios with both classic Scheil and Scheil-with-solute-trapping models for rapidly solidified 316L-type alloys. Both Scheil variants generally **overestimated** the degree of segregation relative to experiments (pqac-00000037). This is consistent with the finding by Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) that Thermo-Calc Scheil simulations for L-PBF 316L show strong Cr and Mo segregation at the end of liquid–solid transformation, but after only 0.1 s the segregation weakens substantially, and after 1 s it is nearly absent, due to the high equilibrium partition coefficients of these elements in austenite (pqac-00000052). This rapid homogenization explains why experimentally measured segregation is weaker than Scheil predicts.

**Oxide inclusions.** The predominant inclusions in as-built LPBF 316L are nanoscale (5–100 nm) Mn- and Si-rich oxide particles, identified as MnO–SiO₂ type (rhodonite, MnSiO₃), located primarily along cell walls (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000007). These particles act as Zener-pinning sites for dislocations (pqac-00000010). Funch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e16555) confirmed that in the as-built state, the particles are primarily Si- and O-rich (amorphous silicates), with average diameters of approximately 50 nm, coarsening to ~100 nm upon annealing at 800 °C (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007).

---

### 4. Etchants and SEM Conditions

Multiple etchants have been documented for revealing cells and melt-pool boundaries in LPBF 316L:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**SEM conditions for microsegregation contrast.** Godec et al. (2020) used electron channelling contrast imaging (ECCI) with a Zeiss Merlin SEM at 30 kV, 2 nA beam current, 7 mm working distance, and a retractable 4-quadrant BSE detector to image dislocation cells and nano-inclusions in bulk polished (unetched) samples (pqac-00000043). For EBSD, the same group used a JEOL 6500F at 15 kV, 1.2 nA, 70° tilt, 4×4 binning (pqac-00000043). BSE imaging at 20 kV was also used by Bauer (2021; DOI: 10.3929/ethz-b-000503119) for melt-pool characterization (pqac-00000046). The key point for the user's experiment (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) is that BSE imaging of unetched sections can directly reveal the cellular microstructure via atomic-number contrast from Mo/Cr segregation, while etching preferentially attacks the composition-different melt-pool boundaries and cell walls.

---

### 5. Thermophysical Properties and the Normalized Enthalpy Keyhole Criterion

The normalized enthalpy criterion, originally formulated by Hann et al. and applied to LPBF by King et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005) on a **Concept Laser M2** machine with 316L (CL 20ES powder), defines the transition to keyhole-mode melting. The normalized enthalpy is:

ΔH/h_s = AP / [h_s √(π D u σ³)]

where A is absorptivity, P is laser power, h_s = ρcT_m is the enthalpy at melting, D is thermal diffusivity, u is scan speed, and σ is the Gaussian beam radius (1/e² standard deviation). The keyhole threshold occurs at ΔH/h_s ≈ π T_b/T_m ≈ 6 (pqac-00000050).

The following table compiles thermophysical properties of 316L from multiple sources:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

The significant variation in reported values (e.g., latent heat ranging from 260 to 330 kJ/kg, thermal diffusivity from 3.25 to 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) underscores that model predictions are sensitive to the chosen property dataset and whether temperature-dependent or constant properties are used. The King et al. values (A = 0.4, h_s = 1.2 × 10⁶ J/kg, D = 5.38 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) are particularly relevant because they were calibrated on the same Concept Laser M2 platform described in the user's experiment (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**What etched SEM sections measure that a CALPHAD-based melt-pool model also predicts.** Etched cross-sections reveal melt-pool width and depth (from the last-layer melt-pool boundaries), which are the same geometric quantities predicted by Rosenthal-based or finite-element melt-pool models using CALPHAD-derived thermophysical properties (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). The normalized enthalpy framework collapses melt-pool depth (normalized by beam size) as a function of ΔH/h_s, enabling direct comparison of predicted and measured melt-pool aspect ratios to identify conduction-mode versus keyhole-mode melting regimes. The Thermo-Calc AM Module generates printability maps in P–v space that delineate lack-of-fusion, keyholing, and balling boundaries; the experimentally measured melt-pool dimensions and porosity from etched sections can be overlaid on these maps for calibration and validation (pqac-00000051).

---

### Summary of Confidence Levels

| Topic | Confidence |
|---|---|
| Equilibrium liquidus/solidus from Thermo-Calc (~1453/1424 °C) | Moderate (single source with specific composition) |
| Primary δ-ferrite solidification for mid-spec 316L (FA mode) | **Strong** (multiple independent CALPHAD and experimental sources) |
| Fully austenitic as-built LPBF 316L (ferrite suppressed) | **Strong** (consistent across XRD, EBSD, TEM studies) |
| Cell spacing λ = 80·Ṫ⁻⁰·³³ with 0.2–0.8 µm range | **Strong** (multiple studies, well-established relation) |
| Creq/Nieq sensitivity within 316L spec (1.01–2.21 range) | **Strong** (Grosswendt et al. with ASTM A276 analysis) |
| Mo enrichment at cell walls (~27% relative to interior) | Moderate (quantitative from one study, qualitative from several) |
| Scheil overestimation of segregation | Moderate (demonstrated for 316L-type alloys, mechanism explained) |
| Keyhole threshold ΔH/h_s ≈ 6 for 316L on Concept Laser M2 | **Strong** (King et al. 2014, >2200 citations, same machine platform) |
| Latent heat and thermal property values | Moderate–weak (significant scatter across sources; values are composition- and database-dependent) |

---

### Key Data Tables and Open Datasets for Comparison

- Godec et al. (2020), Table 3 and Figure 6: quantitative STEM-EDS compositions at cell walls, cell interiors, and melt-pool boundaries (DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074).
- Bertoli et al. (2019), Table 3: G, R, G·R, G/R for three LPBF parameter sets; Table 4: mechanical properties (DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2018.10.051).
- King et al. (2014), Table 3: thermophysical constants for normalized enthalpy; Figure 5: melt-pool depth vs. ΔH/h_s for 316L on Concept Laser M2 at two beam sizes (DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005).
- Grosswendt et al. (2021), Table with Creq/Nieq ratios for three 316L compositions (DOI: 10.3390/ma14154074).
- Wahib (2024), Table 8: Thermo-Calc solidus/liquidus and thermophysical properties for 316L (DOI: 10.34901/mul.pub.2024.074).
- Sotiriou et al. (2021), Table 1: temperature-dependent k and c_p for 316L (DOI: 10.3390/iec2m-09237)."}

## CALPHAD Predictions, LPBF Solidification, and Characterization of 316L Stainless Steel

### 1. CALPHAD Predictions: Liquidus, Solidus, Freezing Range, and Primary Phase

**Equilibrium solidification.** Thermo-Calc calculations for 316L stainless steel using the TCFE database predict an equilibrium liquidus temperature of approximately 1453 °C and a solidus of approximately 1424 °C, yielding a freezing range of about 29 K (wahib2024optimizationofheat pages 59-62). Sotiriou et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/iec2m-09237) used Thermo-Calc with TCFE6 for a nominal 316L composition of Fe–18Cr–14Ni–2.6Mo–1Mn–0.03C (wt%) and adopted a solidus of 1400 °C and liquidus of 1459 °C (a 59 K interval) as model inputs for their heat-transfer simulation, with a latent heat of 330 kJ/kg distributed over that range (sotiriou2021microstructuralandthermomechanical pages 2-4, sotiriou2021microstructuralandthermomechanical pages 4-6). These values differ from the Wahib (2024; DOI: 10.34901/mul.pub.2024.074) Thermo-Calc output because the alloy compositions and databases used are not identical—illustrating the sensitivity of CALPHAD predictions to both input chemistry and database version.

**Scheil–Gulliver solidification.** The Scheil–Gulliver model, which assumes no solid-state diffusion and complete liquid mixing, predicts a wider freezing range than equilibrium because extended solute rejection into the liquid depresses the terminal solidus temperature (sotiriou2021microstructuralandthermomechanical pages 8-9). Sotiriou et al. explicitly stated that the Scheil–Gulliver model yields the highest freezing range, while equilibrium gives the lowest, with DICTRA kinetic simulations falling in between depending on the imposed thermal cycle (sotiriou2021microstructuralandthermomechanical pages 8-9). Assi et al. (2024; DOI: 10.3390/app14198649) defined the "critical temperature range" from Scheil as the interval between 95% and 99% solid fraction, which is the most cracking-sensitive portion of the solidification path (assi2024designandassessment pages 5-7).

**Primary phase: δ-ferrite vs. austenite.** For typical mid-specification 316L compositions (Creq/Nieq ≈ 1.3–1.5), CALPHAD and Scheil calculations predict primary δ-ferrite solidification via the ferrite–austenite (FA) mode: L → L + δ → L + δ + γ → γ + δ (liu2026researchprogresson pages 17-19). Grosswendt et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/ma14154074) used Thermo-Calc Scheil–Gulliver simulations with an Fe–Cr–Ni pseudobinary at 70 mass% Fe and showed that alloys with Creq/Nieq = 1.35 and 1.43 solidify as primary bcc ferrite, while an alloy with Creq/Nieq = 1.00 solidifies as primary fcc austenite (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 11-13).

**Creq/Nieq and composition effects.** The Schaeffler equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 1.4(%Si) + 0.5(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 0.5(%Mn) + 30(%C); the WRC-1992 equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 0.7(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 35(%C) + 20(%N) + 0.25(%Cu) (tonelli2021additivemanufacturingby pages 230-235, liu2026researchprogresson pages 17-19). Within the ASTM A276 316L specification, the permissible Creq/Nieq ratio can range from as low as 1.01 to as high as 2.21, spanning fully austenitic (A) through ferritic–austenitic (FA) solidification regimes (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 15-17). Below approximately 1.3, fully austenitic solidification is expected; above approximately 1.49 (Schaeffler) or 1.59 (Hammar–Svensson), primary ferrite becomes dominant (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 11-13, sutton2021developmentofa pages 34-41). This is a **strongly supported** finding from multiple independent studies. Grosswendt et al. recommend restricting the Ni equivalent and setting Cr to 17–18 mass% for PBF-LB/M to maintain Creq/Nieq > 1.3 and avoid ductility-dip cracking that accompanies fully austenitic solidification (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 15-17).

**Retained ferrite in as-built LPBF 316L.** Despite equilibrium and Scheil predictions of primary δ-ferrite for mid-specification compositions, as-built LPBF 316L is typically fully austenitic with no detectable δ-ferrite by XRD (funch2023thermalstabilityof pages 2-3). This is attributed to the combination of rapid solidification (cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s) and intrinsic reheating from subsequent layer deposition, which enables diffusion-driven transformation of initially solidified ferrite into austenite (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 11-13, liu2026researchprogresson pages 17-19). Grosswendt et al. confirmed that their PBF-LB/M samples A and C were fully austenitic, while sample B retained only a small ferrite fraction (grosswendt2021impactofthe pages 11-13). Some studies have detected trace ferrite by TEM at cell boundaries in SLM 316L (ozel2023microstructureofselective pages 2-5), but the consensus is that the as-built phase is overwhelmingly austenitic. This represents a **strong** finding.

---

### 2. Cellular Sub-Structure: Cell Spacing vs. Cooling Rate

The solidification microstructure of LPBF 316L consists of columnar cellular sub-structures with cell spacings of approximately 0.2–0.8 µm, corresponding to estimated cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s (vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 13-14, fu2021comparisonofthe pages 20-24).

**Empirical relation.** The widely used fitted relation for stainless steels is:

λ (µm) = 80 · Ṫ⁻⁰·³³

where Ṫ is the cooling rate in K/s, a = 80 µm·(K/s)⁰·³³, and n = 0.33 (fu2021comparisonofthe pages 20-24, vallejo2021processoptimizationand pages 13-14, bertoli2019stabilityofcellular pages 5-7). This relation was used by both Fu et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102067) and Vallejo et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11050832) for LPBF 316L, with consistent results.

Bertoli et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2018.10.051) systematically varied LPBF parameters and reported the solidification conditions summarized in the following table:

| Sample # | Laser power (W) | Scan speed (mm/s) | Hatch spacing (mm) | P/v (J/mm) | G (K/mm) | R (mm/s) | Modeled G·R (K/s) | G/R (K·s/mm²) | Measured cell size from micrographs (µm) | Estimated cell size from modeled G·R (µm) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 60 | 30 | 0.120 | 2.00 | 7.9×10³ | 15 | 3.1×10⁵ | 194 | ≈0.88 | 1.23 |
| 2 | 175 | 750 | 0.120 | 0.23 | 1.9×10⁴ | 137 | 2.7×10⁶ | 141 | ≈0.61 | 0.60 |
| 3 | 380 | 2500 | 0.025 | 0.15 | 2.3×10⁴ | 176 | 4.2×10⁶ | 132 | ≈0.50 | 0.52 |
| **Relation** | — | — | — | — | — | — | Cooling rate = G·R | — | Approximate values inferred from the cell-size-derived cooling rates reported by Bertoli et al.: 8.7×10⁵, 2.6×10⁶, and 4.7×10⁶ K/s | λ (µm) = 80·(G·R)^−0.33, with G·R in K/s (bertoli2019stabilityofcellular pages 5-7) |


*Table: LPBF 316L process and modeled solidification conditions reported by Bertoli et al. The comparison shows that increasing cooling rate refines the cellular spacing.*

The cooling rate is inversely proportional to the P/v ratio (linear energy density), confirming that G·R ∝ v/P (bertoli2019stabilityofcellular pages 5-7). The G/R ratio remained within a narrow range of 100–200 K·s/mm² across all tested conditions, which is why only columnar cellular morphology was observed—never equiaxed dendrites (bertoli2019stabilityofcellular pages 5-7).

**Spatial variation within melt pools.** Cell size varies systematically within a single melt pool. Near the melt-pool boundary, where the thermal gradient G is highest and the solidification rate R is lowest, finer cells form ("type 1" cells, 0.20–0.40 µm diameter). Toward the melt-pool center/top, where cooling rates decrease, coarser cells develop ("type 2") (hasenbusch2023acomparisonof pages 19-29). Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) confirmed that G/R decreases from the melt-pool boundary toward the center, promoting a gradual transition from columnar to more equiaxed morphologies (wang2024additivemanufacturinginducedcellstructure pages 4-6). The cells have a 3D prism-like morphology with their long axes aligned along <001> crystallographic directions, and undergo 90° side-branching near melt-pool boundary intersections (wang2024additivemanufacturinginducedcellstructure pages 4-6).

---

### 3. Microsegregation and Oxide Inclusions

**Quantitative STEM-EDS data.** Godec et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074) provided the most detailed quantitative STEM-EDS measurements for LPBF 316L (EOS M280, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, nitrogen atmosphere). At the dislocation-based cell walls (position 3): Cr = 17.4 wt%, Mo = 4.2 wt%, Mn = 1.8 wt%, Ni = 13.7 wt%, Fe = 62.9 wt%. Inside the cell (position 2): Cr = 17.0 wt%, Mo = 3.3 wt%, Mn = 1.7 wt%, Ni = 13.5 wt%, Fe = 64.5 wt%. At the melt-pool boundary (position 1): Cr = 16.6 wt%, Mo = 3.1 wt%, Ni = 13.6 wt%, Fe = 64.9 wt% (godec2020quantitativemultiscalecorrelative pages 14-19). Thus, Mo is the most strongly segregated element, with approximately 27% enrichment at cell walls relative to the cell interior, while Cr shows modest enrichment (~2%) and Ni is essentially uniform. The melt-pool boundary is characterized by a Mo and Cr *deficit* relative to both the cell walls and cell interiors, explaining why even minor composition differences produce a strong etching effect that makes melt-pool boundaries visible under optical microscopy (godec2020quantitativemultiscalecorrelative pages 14-19).

**Comparison with Scheil predictions.** Hasenbusch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1093/micmic/ozad065) compared measured STEM-EDX segregation ratios with both classic Scheil and Scheil-with-solute-trapping models for rapidly solidified 316L-type alloys. Both Scheil variants generally **overestimated** the degree of segregation relative to experiments (hasenbusch2023acomparisonof pages 49-54). This is consistent with the finding by Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) that Thermo-Calc Scheil simulations for L-PBF 316L show strong Cr and Mo segregation at the end of liquid–solid transformation, but after only 0.1 s the segregation weakens substantially, and after 1 s it is nearly absent, due to the high equilibrium partition coefficients of these elements in austenite (wang2024additivemanufacturinginducedcellstructure pages 4-6). This rapid homogenization explains why experimentally measured segregation is weaker than Scheil predicts.

**Oxide inclusions.** The predominant inclusions in as-built LPBF 316L are nanoscale (5–100 nm) Mn- and Si-rich oxide particles, identified as MnO–SiO₂ type (rhodonite, MnSiO₃), located primarily along cell walls (godec2020quantitativemultiscalecorrelative pages 14-19, hasenbusch2023acomparisonof pages 1-6, barode2025cellstructurein pages 4-7). These particles act as Zener-pinning sites for dislocations (hasenbusch2023acomparisonof pages 1-6). Funch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e16555) confirmed that in the as-built state, the particles are primarily Si- and O-rich (amorphous silicates), with average diameters of approximately 50 nm, coarsening to ~100 nm upon annealing at 800 °C (funch2023thermalstabilityof pages 10-13, barode2025cellstructurein pages 4-7).

---

### 4. Etchants and SEM Conditions

Multiple etchants have been documented for revealing cells and melt-pool boundaries in LPBF 316L:

| Etchant name | Composition | Application method and duration | Features revealed | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Glycerine aqua regia (glyceregia) | 20 mL glycerine + 10 mL HNO₃ + 30 mL HCl | Chemical immersion; duration not reported | Cellular/dendritic microstructure and arc-shaped melt-pool boundaries | Godec et al. (2020), DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074 (godec2020quantitativemultiscalecorrelative pages 5-9) |
| Ferric-chloride solution | 5 g FeCl₃ + 10 mL HCl + 100 mL ethanol | Chemical immersion; duration not reported | Melt-pool lines preferentially, rather than the full cellular microstructure | Godec et al. (2020), DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074 (godec2020quantitativemultiscalecorrelative pages 5-9) |
| V2A etchant | Proprietary/standard V2A formulation; exact recipe not reported in the cited passage | Chemical immersion at room temperature for 30–60 s | Melt-pool boundaries, grains, subgrain boundaries, and round-to-elongated cellular structures | Özel et al. ## CALPHAD Predictions, LPBF Solidification, and Characterization of 316L Stainless Steel

### 1. CALPHAD Predictions: Liquidus, Solidus, Freezing Range, and Primary Phase

**Equilibrium solidification.** Thermo-Calc calculations for 316L stainless steel using the TCFE database predict an equilibrium liquidus temperature of approximately 1453 °C and a solidus of approximately 1424 °C, yielding a freezing range of about 29 K (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000020). Sotiriou et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/iec2m-09237) used Thermo-Calc with TCFE6 for a nominal 316L composition of Fe–18Cr–14Ni–2.6Mo–1Mn–0.03C (wt%) and adopted a solidus of 1400 °C and liquidus of 1459 °C (a 59 K interval) as model inputs for their heat-transfer simulation, with a latent heat of 330 kJ/kg distributed over that range (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). These values differ from the Wahib (2024; DOI: 10.34901/mul.pub.2024.074) Thermo-Calc output because the alloy compositions and databases used are not identical—illustrating the sensitivity of CALPHAD predictions to both input chemistry and database version.

**Scheil–Gulliver solidification.** The Scheil–Gulliver model, which assumes no solid-state diffusion and complete liquid mixing, predicts a wider freezing range than equilibrium because extended solute rejection into the liquid depresses the terminal solidus temperature (pqac-00000057). Sotiriou et al. explicitly stated that the Scheil–Gulliver model yields the highest freezing range, while equilibrium gives the lowest, with DICTRA kinetic simulations falling in between depending on the imposed thermal cycle (pqac-00000057). Assi et al. (2024; DOI: 10.3390/app14198649) defined the "critical temperature range" from Scheil as the interval between 95% and 99% solid fraction, which is the most cracking-sensitive portion of the solidification path (pqac-00000061).

**Primary phase: δ-ferrite vs. austenite.** For typical mid-specification 316L compositions (Creq/Nieq ≈ 1.3–1.5), CALPHAD and Scheil calculations predict primary δ-ferrite solidification via the ferrite–austenite (FA) mode: L → L + δ → L + δ + γ → γ + δ (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000031). Grosswendt et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/ma14154074) used Thermo-Calc Scheil–Gulliver simulations with an Fe–Cr–Ni pseudobinary at 70 mass% Fe and showed that alloys with Creq/Nieq = 1.35 and 1.43 solidify as primary bcc ferrite, while an alloy with Creq/Nieq = 1.00 solidifies as primary fcc austenite (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000053).

**Creq/Nieq and composition effects.** The Schaeffler equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 1.4(%Si) + 0.5(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 0.5(%Mn) + 30(%C); the WRC-1992 equivalents are Creq = %Cr + %Mo + 0.7(%Nb) and Nieq = %Ni + 35(%C) + 20(%N) + 0.25(%Cu) (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031). Within the ASTM A276 316L specification, the permissible Creq/Nieq ratio can range from as low as 1.01 to as high as 2.21, spanning fully austenitic (A) through ferritic–austenitic (FA) solidification regimes (pqac-00000033). Below approximately 1.3, fully austenitic solidification is expected; above approximately 1.49 (Schaeffler) or 1.59 (Hammar–Svensson), primary ferrite becomes dominant (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034). This is a **strongly supported** finding from multiple independent studies. Grosswendt et al. recommend restricting the Ni equivalent and setting Cr to 17–18 mass% for PBF-LB/M to maintain Creq/Nieq > 1.3 and avoid ductility-dip cracking that accompanies fully austenitic solidification (pqac-00000033).

**Retained ferrite in as-built LPBF 316L.** Despite equilibrium and Scheil predictions of primary δ-ferrite for mid-specification compositions, as-built LPBF 316L is typically fully austenitic with no detectable δ-ferrite by XRD (pqac-00000025). This is attributed to the combination of rapid solidification (cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s) and intrinsic reheating from subsequent layer deposition, which enables diffusion-driven transformation of initially solidified ferrite into austenite (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000026). Grosswendt et al. confirmed that their PBF-LB/M samples A and C were fully austenitic, while sample B retained only a small ferrite fraction (pqac-00000030). Some studies have detected trace ferrite by TEM at cell boundaries in SLM 316L (pqac-00000038), but the consensus is that the as-built phase is overwhelmingly austenitic. This represents a **strong** finding.

---

### 2. Cellular Sub-Structure: Cell Spacing vs. Cooling Rate

The solidification microstructure of LPBF 316L consists of columnar cellular sub-structures with cell spacings of approximately 0.2–0.8 µm, corresponding to estimated cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000002).

**Empirical relation.** The widely used fitted relation for stainless steels is:

λ (µm) = 80 · Ṫ⁻⁰·³³

where Ṫ is the cooling rate in K/s, a = 80 µm·(K/s)⁰·³³, and n = 0.33 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000039). This relation was used by both Fu et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102067) and Vallejo et al. (2021; DOI: 10.3390/met11050832) for LPBF 316L, with consistent results.

Bertoli et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1016/j.msea.2018.10.051) systematically varied LPBF parameters and reported the solidification conditions summarized in the following table:

|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 60 | 30 | 0.120 | 2.00 | 7.9×10³ | 15 | 3.1×10⁵ | 194 | ≈0.88 | 1.23 |

*Table: LPBF 316L process and modeled solidification conditions reported by Bertoli et al. The comparison shows that increasing cooling rate refines the cellular spacing.*

The cooling rate is inversely proportional to the P/v ratio (linear energy density), confirming that G·R ∝ v/P (pqac-00000039). The G/R ratio remained within a narrow range of 100–200 K·s/mm² across all tested conditions, which is why only columnar cellular morphology was observed—never equiaxed dendrites (pqac-00000039).

**Spatial variation within melt pools.** Cell size varies systematically within a single melt pool. Near the melt-pool boundary, where the thermal gradient G is highest and the solidification rate R is lowest, finer cells form ("type 1" cells, 0.20–0.40 µm diameter). Toward the melt-pool center/top, where cooling rates decrease, coarser cells develop ("type 2") (pqac-00000042). Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) confirmed that G/R decreases from the melt-pool boundary toward the center, promoting a gradual transition from columnar to more equiaxed morphologies (pqac-00000052). The cells have a 3D prism-like morphology with their long axes aligned along <001> crystallographic directions, and undergo 90° side-branching near melt-pool boundary intersections (pqac-00000052).

### 3. Microsegregation and Oxide Inclusions

**Quantitative STEM-EDS data.** Godec et al. (2020; DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2019.110074) provided the most detailed quantitative STEM-EDS measurements for LPBF 316L (EOS M280, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, nitrogen atmosphere). At the dislocation-based cell walls (position 3): Cr = 17.4 wt%, Mo = 4.2 wt%, Mn = 1.8 wt%, Ni = 13.7 wt%, Fe = 62.9 wt%. Inside the cell (position 2): Cr = 17.0 wt%, Mo = 3.3 wt%, Mn = 1.7 wt%, Ni = 13.5 wt%, Fe = 64.5 wt%. At the melt-pool boundary (position 1): Cr = 16.6 wt%, Mo = 3.1 wt%, Ni = 13.6 wt%, Fe = 64.9 wt% (pqac-00000044). Thus, Mo is the most strongly segregated element, with approximately 27% enrichment at cell walls relative to the cell interior, while Cr shows modest enrichment (~2%) and Ni is essentially uniform. The melt-pool boundary is characterized by a Mo and Cr *deficit* relative to both the cell walls and cell interiors, explaining why even minor composition differences produce a strong etching effect that makes melt-pool boundaries visible under optical microscopy (pqac-00000044).

**Comparison with Scheil predictions.** Hasenbusch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1093/micmic/ozad065) compared measured STEM-EDX segregation ratios with both classic Scheil and Scheil-with-solute-trapping models for rapidly solidified 316L-type alloys. Both Scheil variants generally **overestimated** the degree of segregation relative to experiments (pqac-00000037). This is consistent with the finding by Wang et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1007/s11661-024-07644-w) that Thermo-Calc Scheil simulations for L-PBF 316L show strong Cr and Mo segregation at the end of liquid–solid transformation, but after only 0.1 s the segregation weakens substantially, and after 1 s it is nearly absent, due to the high equilibrium partition coefficients of these elements in austenite (pqac-00000052). This rapid homogenization explains why experimentally measured segregation is weaker than Scheil predicts.

**Oxide inclusions.** The predominant inclusions in as-built LPBF 316L are nanoscale (5–100 nm) Mn- and Si-rich oxide particles, identified as MnO–SiO₂ type (rhodonite, MnSiO₃), located primarily along cell walls (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000007). These particles act as Zener-pinning sites for dislocations (pqac-00000010). Funch et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e16555) confirmed that in the as-built state, the particles are primarily Si- and O-rich (amorphous silicates), with average diameters of approximately 50 nm, coarsening to ~100 nm upon annealing at 800 °C (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000007).

The significant variation in reported values (e.g., latent heat ranging from 260 to 330 kJ/kg, thermal diffusivity from 3.25 to 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) underscores that model predictions are sensitive to the chosen property dataset and whether temperature-dependent or constant properties are used. The King et al. values (A = 0.4, h_s = 1.2 × 10⁶ J/kg, D = 5.38 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) are particularly relevant because they were calibrated on the same Concept Laser M2 platform described in the user's experiment (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**What etched SEM sections measure that a CALPHAD-based melt-pool model also predicts.** Etched cross-sections reveal melt-pool width and depth (from the last-layer melt-pool boundaries), which are the same geometric quantities predicted by Rosenthal-based or finite-element melt-pool models using CALPHAD-derived thermophysical properties (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). The normalized enthalpy framework collapses melt-pool depth (normalized by beam size) as a function of ΔH/h_s, enabling direct comparison of predicted and measured melt-pool aspect ratios to identify conduction-mode versus keyhole-mode melting regimes. The Thermo-Calc AM Module generates printability maps in P–v space that delineate lack-of-fusion, keyholing, and balling boundaries; the experimentally measured melt-pool dimensions and porosity from etched sections can be overlaid on these maps for calibration and validation (pqac-00000051).

contexts.context: This excerpt describes the TEM STEM-EDX methodology used to assess cellular microsegregation, including the LPBF alloy 1 sample, which corresponds to a 316L stainless-steel composition. Elemental line scans were collected across individual solidification cells. Signal intensity ratios relative to Fe were used qualitatively to compensate for sample-thickness variations and to identify cell boundaries and segregation regions, but the reported segregation ratios for individual elements were based on each element’s integrated, background-subtracted X-ray intensity rather than element/Fe ratios. The average intensity at the cell center represented the initial or cell-interior composition (CS), while the intensity at the cell boundary represented the final-solidifying composition (CL). Simulation segregation ratios used the initial composition and final solidified composition, rather than the equilibrium partition coefficient under rapid-solidification conditions. However, the supplied pages do not provide numerical Cr, Mo, Ni, or Si enrichments at LPBF cell walls, any APT measurements, direct Scheil-prediction comparisons, or information about oxide inclusions. Those results must therefore come from other sections of the article.

Qualitatively, 316L is described as commonly solidifying in the ferrite–austenite (FA) mode through L → L + δ → L + δ + γ → γ + δ, leaving a small amount of residual δ-ferrite. Composition changes that increase Cr, Mo, or Nb raise Creq and promote ferrite, while increases in Ni, C, N, or Cu raise Nieq and promote a more austenitic path. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide explicit Schaeffler or WRC-1992 equations, nor does it tabulate separate Creq/Nieq values for ASTM A240. It does show how composition variation within the ASTM A276-type 316L range changes the chromium-equivalent/nickel-equivalent balance and therefore the solidification behavior. For the proposed PBF-LB/M composition range, the reported Creq/Nieq values extend from 1.28 to 2.21, while the broader ASTM A276 range can produce a minimum ratio of 1.01 and the same maximum of 2.21. The authors recommend a ratio above 1.3 to prevent ductility-dip cracking (DDCs). Increasing carbon and nitrogen raises Nieq through interstitial solid-solution effects; the excerpt states that C and N increase Nieq much more strongly than Ni. A higher Nieq lowers Creq/Nieq, promoting a more austenitic solidification tendency and increasing susceptibility to DDCs, whereas restricting Ni and narrowing Cr to 17–18 mass% raises the ratio and favors avoidance of cracking. Thus, specification limits can span materially different solidification modes, but the excerpt alone does not establish exact Schaeffler/WRC-1992 classifications or ASTM A240-specific extrema.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the Schaeffler or WRC-1992 Creq/Nieq formulas, nor does it give a specific 316L composition or numerical Creq/Nieq ratios. It does, however, explain how composition variation can affect predicted solidification mode. Calculations across 11,000 randomized stainless-steel compositions showed a generally linear separation between primary-austenite and primary-ferrite regions when plotted in WRC equivalency space, with a narrow mixed-prediction region near the transition. The study introduced two composition-sensitive solidification metrics. In the Scheil-based metric, ΔfS is based on the solid fractions at which ferrite and austenite first form; ΔfS is positive for primary-austenite alloys and negative for primary-ferrite alloys, while zero marks the transition. In the equilibrium/metastable approach, ΔTL is the difference between austenite and ferrite liquidus temperatures; positive values indicate primary-austenite stability, negative values primary-ferrite stability, and zero the transition. Therefore, compositions lying near the limits of the ASTM 316L specification could potentially shift their predicted mode or move closer to the austenite/ferrite boundary, but the excerpt supplies no 316L-specific calculations or quantitative comparison.
